title: Right to be forgotten
brief: 16:45. A former customer has closed his account and wants every trace of him deleted. Some of it can go. Some of it must stay.
role: Accounts payable, covering the customer privacy inbox tonight
insight: Erasure is a real right, but not an absolute one. The law that makes you keep invoices still applies, and backups are not a hiding place.
teaches: Delete what you no longer need; keep what the law requires, and say so
Backups count: stop the data being restored, and let it age out
Tell the suppliers you shared it with to erase it too

value.title: Erasure request: {{name}}
body: “I have closed my account. Please delete all the personal data you hold about me, and confirm when it is done.”
Identity is confirmed: the request came from his verified account email. Here is what we hold.

policy.title: Veltrix retention schedule (extract)
lines: Sales invoices and payment records: keep 6 years from the end of the financial year, for tax law.
Marketing data: delete when consent is withdrawn.
Backups: 35 day rolling cycle. Erased records must not be restored from backup.

options.label: Delete
options.why: He has withdrawn. Nothing requires keeping it.

options.label: Keep, in case he comes back
options.why: “In case” is not a reason. It has to go.

sections.title: His invoices and payment records from 2025

options.label: Keep until 2032, as tax law requires, and tell him why
options.why: A legal obligation overrides erasure for these records. Explaining it is part of the answer.

options.label: Delete them, he asked for everything
options.why: Deleting records the law requires you to keep swaps one breach for another.

options.label: Delete
options.why: Past the 2 year retention, and no reason to keep them.

options.label: Keep, they might be useful for training
options.why: Not a lawful reason to keep someone's chats after they asked for erasure.

sections.title: Last month's backups, which include his records

options.label: Record that his data must never be restored, and let the backups age out in 35 days
options.why: Backups are not exempt, but you do not have to rebuild them: stop restores, let them expire.

options.label: Leave them, backups do not count
options.why: Backups do count. Restore one, and he is back in the live system.

options.label: Restore every backup, edit him out, and back them up again
options.why: Risky and unnecessary. Putting them beyond use is enough.

sections.title: Delivery data shared with Dropwell Couriers

options.label: Ask Dropwell to erase his data too
options.why: Suppliers processing it for you must be told.

options.label: Nothing, it is their data now
options.why: They hold it on your behalf. His request reaches them through you.

actions.label: Carry it out and confirm to the customer

choices.label: An erasure request. Do the invoices and backups have to go too?

script.say: Invoices stay, tax law wins, but tell him that. Backups: flag him so he is never restored, and let them roll off. And tell Dropwell.

setup.title: Work queue
setup.body: A former customer wants his data deleted

outcome.label: Checked with data protection
outcome.what: Invoices stay, backups are flagged, suppliers are told.
outcome.ideal: asks the DPO about exceptions before acting.

outcome.label: Did not let the backups off the hook
outcome.what: Flagged so he is never restored, and left to expire.
outcome.ideal: treats backups as part of erasure.

outcome.label: Passed the request on to the courier
outcome.what: Dropwell holds his addresses for you, so they erase them too.

decide.objective: Work out what to erase and what to keep, then confirm to the customer.
decide.insight: Delete what you no longer need. Keep only what the law requires, and tell him what and why.

hint.text: Open the Work queue and read the retention schedule. Delete marketing and old support chats, keep the invoices for tax, flag the backups, tell Dropwell. Data protection is on 4120.

outcome.label: Erased what could go, kept what must stay
outcome.what: Marketing and support data gone, invoices kept for tax with an explanation, backups flagged, Dropwell told.
outcome.ideal: applies erasure with its legal exceptions, including backups and suppliers.

card.title: Gone, except what the law keeps
body: Everything you no longer needed is gone. The invoices stay until 2032 because tax law requires them, and he has been told why. His data will not come back from a backup, and Dropwell has been asked to erase its copy.
Erasure is not “delete everything” and not “delete nothing”. It is a record by record decision.
card.ideal: deletes what can go, keeps what must stay, and explains.

outcome.label: Deleted records the law requires
outcome.what: The invoices had to be kept for tax. Deleting them trades one compliance problem for another.
outcome.ideal: keeps records a legal obligation requires, and explains that to the requester.

card.title: Too much, gone
body: His 2025 invoices had to be kept for six years under tax law. The right to erasure does not override a legal obligation to keep a record.
The answer was to keep them, and tell him so.
card.ideal: checks the retention schedule before erasing.

outcome.label: Confirmed an erasure that was not complete
outcome.what: Something he asked to be erased is still there: in marketing, support, a backup, or with the courier.
outcome.ideal: erases everything not covered by an exception, including backups and suppliers.

card.title: Confirmed, but not true
body: You told him it was done, but some of his data is still there, or could come back from a backup. Open the case to see which records were missed.
Backups are not a free pass, and suppliers holding data for you have to be told.
card.ideal: follows the data everywhere it went.
